Dispensationalists answer that the new covenant was made with 'the house of Israel and the house of Judah' (Jeremiah 31:31) and, while the church shares its spiritual blessings now, its national and land promises (Ezekiel 36:28) await Israel. They note that Ezekiel 36:22 grounds the return in God's name, not Israel's repentance, which explains a return before faith.
The order of verses gives the futurist reading a foothold; the New Testament's use of this new-covenant text for the church gives the fulfilment reading its strength.

Jesus says Jerusalem will be trampled by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled. Many saw Israel's capture of East Jerusalem in 1967 as the end, or the beginning of the end, of those times.
L. Nelson Bell (Christianity Today, 1967), Hal Lindsey, and many popular prophecy teachers; some dispensational scholars such as John Walvoord used the text more cautiously.

The verse sets a limit: the Gentile trampling of Jerusalem lasts 'until' a set time. If Jerusalem coming under Jewish rule in 1967 ended that trampling, the prophetic clock is near its end. Proponents also read 'until' as implying a reversal for Jerusalem and the Jewish people after the times of the Gentiles.

Critics note that Luke 21:20-24 describes the Roman siege of AD 70: armies surrounding Jerusalem, flight to the mountains, death by the sword and captivity among all nations. The verse predicts the long period of Gentile rule that followed, not a date for its end. Many dispensationalists themselves did not treat 1967 as the end of the times of the Gentiles, since the Temple Mount remained under Muslim religious administration and they place the end of these times at Christ's return (linking it with Daniel 2 and Revelation 11:2). So the verse does not clearly point to 1967.

Proponents answer that 'until' implies an end to Jerusalem's trampling and therefore a future for the city in God's plan; this is also the view of some non-dispensational scholars who see a hint of restoration here. Even if 1967 is not the end of the times of the Gentiles, they see it as a sign that the end is approaching.
The verse does imply a limit to Gentile control of Jerusalem; whether 1967 marks that limit is disputed even among dispensationalists.
God will make Jerusalem a cup of trembling and a heavy stone for all the nations; all who lift it will be hurt. This is read as the modern international struggle over Jerusalem.
Hal Lindsey, John Hagee, Randall Price and many prophecy teachers, often quoted at times of diplomatic debate over Jerusalem.

Proponents note how often Jerusalem has been at the centre of world diplomacy since 1948 and especially since 1967: UN resolutions, peace plans, and disputes over the holy places. They see this as the nations gathering against Jerusalem as Zechariah says (12:3). The same chapter promises that the house of David will look on the one they pierced and mourn (12:10), which they place in the future, after the regathering.

Fulfilment scholars note that Zechariah 12-14 uses battle images to describe God defending His people and the coming of the pierced one. The New Testament applies Zechariah 12:10 to the crucifixion (John 19:37) and to Christ's coming (Revelation 1:7), and the fountain for cleansing (Zechariah 13:1) to His saving work. The 'Jerusalem' of the new covenant is often the people of God (Hebrews 12:22; Galatians 4:26). Critics add that political dispute over a city is not unique to the modern era: Jerusalem was fought over by Crusaders, Mamluks and Ottomans as well.

Proponents answer that Zechariah describes an actual siege of the actual city by 'all the nations of the earth' (12:3), which has not yet happened, and that the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem mourning together (12:10-14) is a national event for Israel. They read John 19:37 as a first fulfilment of the piercing, with the national mourning still future.
A real end-time hope for many; but present diplomatic disputes do not by themselves show which reading is right.

God's promise to Abram, 'I will bless those who bless you and curse him who curses you', is applied to the modern State of Israel: nations and people who support it will be blessed, and those who oppose it cursed.
John Hagee and Christians United for Israel, Jerry Falwell, and many Christian Zionist ministries; Arnold Fruchtenbaum argues that the promise extends to Abraham's physical descendants.

The promise is part of the everlasting Abrahamic covenant. It is repeated for Jacob (Genesis 27:29) and for Israel as a nation through Balaam's oracle (Numbers 24:9), so it is not limited to Abram personally. Proponents argue that God has kept His word in history: empires that persecuted the Jews have fallen. On this view, Christians and nations have a duty to support Israel.

Critics note that the 'you' in Genesis 12:3 is singular, addressed to Abram, and that the climax of the promise is that 'all families of the earth' will be blessed in him. Paul says this promise was the gospel announced in advance, fulfilled when Gentiles are justified by faith in Christ, the seed of Abraham (Galatians 3:8, 16, 29). The promise concerns Abraham and his seed, not any particular government, and applying it to the policies of a modern secular state is a further step the New Testament does not take. Critics also warn that it can silence moral judgment about any state's actions.

Proponents answer that Genesis 27:29 and Numbers 24:9 extend the promise to Abraham's physical line, and that Paul's application to Gentiles in Galatians 3 does not cancel the promise to Israel (Romans 11:28-29). Many careful Christian Zionists apply it to the Jewish people rather than to every action of a government, and accept that Israel can be criticised like any state.
A true covenant promise; whether it applies to the policies of a modern state, rather than to Abraham's seed fulfilled in Christ, is the point in dispute.

God says He will gather all nations into the valley of Jehoshaphat and judge them because they scattered His people and divided up His land. This is applied to modern peace plans that would divide the land, with warnings of judgment on nations that support them.
Bill Koenig (Eye to Eye: Facing the Consequences of Dividing Israel, 2004), John Hagee, and many Christian Zionist commentators on peace negotiations.

The text names dividing God's land as a reason for judging the nations. Proponents argue that the land belongs to God and was given to Israel for ever (Genesis 17:8; Leviticus 25:23), so any division of it, including land-for-peace proposals, falls under this warning. Some point to natural disasters that coincided with such proposals as signs of judgment.

Critics note that Joel 3:1-6 describes nations who had already scattered Israel among the nations, divided the land, cast lots for the people and sold Judah's children to the Greeks. The setting is judgment on Israel's ancient oppressors (Tyre, Sidon, Philistia) after the exile, not modern diplomacy. Peter applies Joel's prophecy of the Spirit (Joel 2:28-32) to Pentecost (Acts 2:16-21), so Joel's 'last days' began then. Critics also say that linking particular disasters to policy decisions is speculation the text does not support.

Proponents answer that Joel 3 is set in 'those days', when the LORD restores Judah's fortunes (3:1), and climaxes in a final judgment of all nations, which has not yet happened. They hold that the principle, that God judges those who divide His land, applies wherever the act is repeated. More cautious futurists accept that the disaster links are speculative while keeping the principle.
The text condemns ancient oppressors and points to final judgment; its use against modern negotiations is an application that most scholars, including many futurists, treat with caution.

Ezekiel foretells an invasion of the restored land by Gog of the land of Magog, with allies, after Israel has been regathered and is living securely. Proponents read this as a future invasion of the modern state, often led by Russia.
Hal Lindsey, John Walvoord, and more recently Joel C. Rosenberg (Epicenter, 2006) and Mark Hitchcock.

Ezekiel 38:8 speaks of a land restored from the sword and gathered from many peoples on the mountains of Israel, which proponents see as matching modern Israel. Gog comes from 'the uttermost parts of the north' (38:6, 15), and Lindsey and others linked 'Rosh' with Russia, Meshech with Moscow and Tubal with Tobolsk. Allies such as Persia (38:5) are read as modern Iran. They expect God to defeat this invasion supernaturally.

Critics note that 'Rosh' is most likely the Hebrew word for 'chief' ('chief prince of Meshech and Tubal'), and Meshech and Tubal are known from Assyrian records as peoples of Anatolia (modern Turkey), not Russia; the sound-alike links with Moscow and Tobolsk have no linguistic basis. Revelation 20:8-9 uses Gog and Magog as a symbol for the final rebellion of the nations against the saints, which suggests a symbolic end-time reading. Critics add that confident identifications have shifted with world events: from Russia in the Cold War to other alliances after 1991, which shows the risk of reading the news into the text.

Some dispensational scholars defend 'Rosh' as a proper name, following the Greek Septuagint, and still see a northern power. More careful futurists now avoid the Moscow and Tobolsk links and say only that the invasion is future, its nations to be identified when it happens. They hold that Ezekiel 38-39 must follow Israel's regathering, which places it after 1948 or later.
A genuine end-time text whose details are hard; the specific modern identifications have often changed with the news.

Love for the Jewish people is not a side issue in this debate. Jesus was a Jew, the apostles were Jews, and the church owes its Scriptures and its Messiah to Israel (Romans 9:4-5). Yet the history of Christian treatment of Jews includes terrible sins: slanders such as the charge of 'deicide', medieval blood libels, expulsions from England (1290) and Spain (1492), Luther's late writings against the Jews, and church silence or complicity during the Holocaust. Paul warns Gentile believers not to boast over the natural branches (Romans 11:18-20), and says that as regards God's choice the Jewish people are 'beloved for the fathers' sakes', for God's gifts and calling are irrevocable (Romans 11:28-29). Christians of every view should therefore speak with humility and care. To question whether a verse predicts 1948 is a question about interpretation. It is not hostility to Jewish people, and it is not a denial of the right of Jews, or of Palestinians, to live in safety and dignity. Equally, supporting the State of Israel does not require one to hold that it fulfils prophecy, and believing it fulfils prophecy does not settle questions of justice. It is also worth knowing that the prophetic reading of the state is debated within Judaism. Many leading Orthodox rabbis opposed political Zionism from the 1890s onward, holding that Jews should not create a state before the Messiah comes. Rabbi Joel Teitelbaum, the Satmar Rebbe, argued this at length in Vayoel Moshe (1961), and the small group Neturei Karta continues to oppose the state on religious grounds. Religious Zionists, following Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook, took the opposite view. Christians therefore should not assume that one reading of 1948 is 'the Jewish view'.

This section asks one question: is the kingdom of Christ already reigning, or is its main earthly form still future? The present-kingdom reading (covenant amillennialists, postmillennialists, preterists and progressive covenantalists) holds that Jesus inaugurated the kingdom in his ministry, took David's throne at his resurrection and ascension, poured out the Spirit at Pentecost as the sign of that reign, and will consummate it at his return in a new heavens and new earth, with no separate political stage in between. The future-kingdom reading (classic and progressive dispensationalists, historic premillennialists and Christian Zionists) holds that Scripture also promises a literal kingdom on this earth after the return of Christ, a thousand-year reign centred in Jerusalem, in which a restored and converted Israel has a distinct and leading place among the nations. Both sides share real common ground. Since George Ladd and Oscar Cullmann almost all evangelical scholars speak of an 'already / not yet' kingdom: Christ reigns now, yet evil, death and the curse are not yet removed. The difference is where each side places the 'not yet'. The present-kingdom reading places it in one event, the return of Christ, which brings resurrection, judgment and the new creation together. Historic premillennialists place it in two stages: a millennium on this earth after the return, then the eternal state. Dispensationalists add that the millennium fulfils the specific national promises made to Israel, especially the Davidic throne in Jerusalem, which they hold Christ has not yet taken in the sense the prophets meant.
The time is fulfilled: the kingdom has drawn near

Jesus opens his preaching in Mark 1:15 with two linked statements: the appointed time has been fulfilled, and the kingdom of God has come near. The present-kingdom reading holds that 'the time' is the time the prophets looked for, the time Daniel 2 and Daniel 7 set for the kingdom of God. Paul uses the same language when he says God sent his Son 'when the fullness of the time had come' (Galatians 4:4). On this reading the arrival of Jesus is not an offer of a kingdom that might be postponed. It is the start of the kingdom the prophets announced.

Dispensationalists such as Pentecost and Walvoord answer that 'has drawn near' (Greek engiken) means 'is close at hand', not 'has arrived'. The kingdom was offered to Israel in the person of the King. When the nation rejected him (Matthew 12; Matthew 23), the earthly form of that kingdom was postponed, and a 'mystery form' of the kingdom began in the church age. Progressive dispensationalists (Blaising and Bock) accept a real inauguration but say the national, Davidic stage is still to come.

Present-kingdom writers (Ridderbos, Hoekema) reply that the Gospels show no postponement. Jesus never says the kingdom he preached is withdrawn; he says it will be taken from the leaders and given to others (Matthew 21:43), which is transfer, not delay. They also note that progressive dispensationalists themselves now grant that the Davidic reign has begun, which weakens the classic postponement idea. The question that remains is whether a later political phase is taught, not whether the kingdom has started.
Acts 1:6-7: Jesus does not deny the restoration to Israel

After forty days of teaching about the kingdom (Acts 1:3), the apostles ask whether Jesus will now restore the kingdom to Israel (Acts 1:6). Jesus does not correct the content of the question; he says only that the times and seasons are set by the Father (Acts 1:7). Peter later speaks of 'times of refreshing' and 'the restoration of all things' that the prophets announced, which come when Christ returns from heaven (Acts 3:19-21). Future-kingdom writers (Saucy, Vlach, Blaising and Bock) hold that this assumes a real future restoration of Israel's kingdom, still to come at the return.

Present-kingdom writers answer that Jesus redirects the question in Acts 1:8: the disciples will receive power and be witnesses from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth. In Luke and Acts the restoration of Israel begins with the gathering of the remnant and the outpouring of the Spirit (Acts 2; Acts 15:16-17, where James sees Amos 9 fulfilled in Gentile conversion). The 'restoration of all things' in Acts 3:21 is the renewal of all creation, not a national stage.

Future-kingdom writers reply that Jesus answers 'when', not 'whether'; if the hope were wrong, after forty days of teaching he could have said so, as he corrected other errors. They argue that Acts 1:8 describes the task in the meantime, not a replacement of the hope. Progressive dispensationalists see Acts 15 as a first stage of the Davidic restoration, with the national stage still ahead.
The kingdom has come upon you, and it is among you

In Matthew 12:28 Jesus says that if he casts out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon his hearers (Greek ephthasen, 'has arrived'). In the next verse he describes binding the strong man and plundering his house (Matthew 12:29). In Luke 17:20-21 he tells the Pharisees that the kingdom does not come with signs to be watched for, because it is already 'in your midst'. The present-kingdom reading holds that these sayings show the kingdom present in the person and works of Jesus, before the cross and long before any future millennium.

Future-kingdom writers agree that the power of the kingdom was present in Jesus. Ladd himself called this 'the presence of the future'. But they argue that a present display of kingdom power is not the same as the full reign over the nations that the prophets describe. In Luke 19:11-27 Jesus tells a parable precisely because people thought the kingdom would appear at once: the nobleman goes away to receive a kingdom and then returns to rule.

The present-kingdom reading agrees that the full display awaits the return, which is the 'not yet'. Its point is that the kingdom Jesus brought is the same kingdom that will be consummated, not a different, spiritual substitute for a later political one. In the parable of Luke 19 the nobleman receives the kingdom while he is away, which fits a reign received at the ascension and made visible at the return, with no further intermediate stage.
Matthew 19:28: the twelve on thrones judging Israel

Jesus promises that 'in the regeneration', when the Son of Man sits on his glorious throne, the twelve apostles will sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matthew 19:28; compare Luke 22:28-30, where he also appoints them a kingdom). Future-kingdom writers hold that this assumes the twelve tribes as a real, identifiable people in the age to come, with the apostles ruling over a restored Israel. They place this at the return of Christ (Matthew 25:31 uses the same phrase about the Son of Man sitting on his glorious throne).

Present-kingdom writers agree that this is future, at the 'regeneration' (Greek palingenesia), but they read the regeneration as the renewal of the whole creation at the return, not a thousand-year interim. Some (France, Beale) also see the twelve tribes as the renewed people of God, as in Revelation 21:12-14, where the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles are both built into the one city.

Future-kingdom writers reply that the regeneration may include the millennium as its first phase, and that 'judging' in the Old Testament sense means ruling, which implies an ongoing government rather than a single act. They argue that the twelve tribes are distinct from the twelve apostles in Revelation 21, which supports a continuing Israelite identity in the age to come.
A kingdom not from this world

Before Pilate, Jesus says his kingdom is not from this world; if it were, his servants would fight to stop his arrest (John 18:36). Paul describes the kingdom as righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit, not food and drink (Romans 14:17). Jesus refused to be made king by force after the feeding of the five thousand (John 6:15). The present-kingdom reading holds that these texts describe the character of Christ's kingdom: it advances by truth, the Spirit and the gospel, not by armies, borders or a political capital.

Dispensationalists answer that 'not from this world' speaks of the kingdom's source and authority, not its location. The kingdom comes from heaven but will be set up on earth, as Jesus taught his disciples to pray: 'your kingdom come, your will be done on earth' (Matthew 6:10). Saucy and Vlach stress that a heavenly origin does not rule out a literal political reign; Daniel 2:44 itself says God will set up a kingdom that breaks the earthly kingdoms.

Present-kingdom writers accept that the kingdom will fill the earth, but in the new creation, not in a restored political order in the old one. They note that in John 18:36 Jesus links 'not of this world' directly with the absence of armed force; the kingdom's nature, not only its source, is in view. Romans 14:17 also defines what the kingdom is, and it is written to a mixed church of Jews and Gentiles about its present life.
Luke 1:32-33: the throne of David over the house of Jacob

Gabriel tells Mary that God will give her son the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob for ever (Luke 1:32-33). Future-kingdom writers note that Mary would have understood this in its Old Testament sense: an earthly throne in Jerusalem over the nation of Israel (2 Samuel 7:16; Jeremiah 33:17). Zechariah's song in the same chapter speaks of salvation 'from our enemies' (Luke 1:71-74). Walvoord and Pentecost hold that such words must be fulfilled in the same sense in which they were given, and that this happens in the millennial kingdom.

Present-kingdom writers answer that Luke himself shows how this promise is fulfilled: Acts 2:30-36 places the Davidic enthronement at the resurrection and ascension. The 'house of Jacob' over which he reigns is the restored Israel of Luke and Acts, the believing remnant into which Gentiles are gathered. A promise 'for ever' cannot be fulfilled by a thousand-year reign; it requires the eternal kingdom.

Future-kingdom writers reply that the millennium is not the whole of the 'for ever' reign; it is its earthly first phase, continuing into the eternal state. Progressive dispensationalists accept that Acts 2 begins the fulfilment but argue that 'over the house of Jacob' still awaits Israel's national repentance (Romans 11:26), so the fulfilment is real now and complete later.
Peter: the resurrection is the enthronement on David's throne

In Acts 2:30-36 Peter says David, as a prophet, knew God had sworn to seat one of his descendants on his throne, and that David foresaw and spoke of the resurrection of the Messiah. Peter then says Jesus has been exalted to the right hand of God, quotes Psalms 110:1, and concludes that God has made him both Lord and Christ. The present-kingdom reading holds that Peter explicitly connects the oath of 2 Samuel 7 and Psalms 132:11 to the resurrection and ascension. The throne of David is being occupied now, at God's right hand.

Classic dispensationalists (Walvoord, Pentecost) distinguish the throne of God, where Christ now sits (Revelation 3:21), from the throne of David, which is an earthly throne in Jerusalem he will take at his return (Matthew 25:31). Peter, they say, shows that the resurrection qualifies Jesus to sit on David's throne, not that he now sits on it. Progressive dispensationalists (Bock, Blaising) disagree with their older colleagues here and accept that Acts 2 teaches a present Davidic reign, but they add that the Jerusalem stage of that reign is still future.

Present-kingdom writers answer that Peter's argument only works if the ascension is the fulfilment of the oath: David spoke of the resurrection 'foreseeing' the seating on his throne (Acts 2:30-31). They welcome Bock's concession as strong support from within the dispensational tradition. They add that Psalms 110:1 is itself a Davidic psalm about the Lord's king, so the right hand of God is the Davidic throne, now raised to its true height.
Isaiah 11 and 65: conditions that fit neither now nor eternity

Isaiah 11:6-9 describes the wolf living with the lamb and the earth full of the knowledge of the Lord. Isaiah 65:20 says a person who dies at a hundred will be thought young, and a sinner who reaches a hundred will be accursed. Future-kingdom writers argue that these conditions are not present today, yet they cannot describe the eternal state either, because death and sin still occur (Revelation 21:4 says death will be no more). So they fit best in a millennial kingdom on this earth, after the return of Christ but before the final new creation.

Present-kingdom writers (Riddlebarger, Motyer, Hoekema) answer that Isaiah 65:20 sits inside a passage that begins with 'new heavens and a new earth' (Isaiah 65:17), which the New Testament places after the final judgment (2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:1). Isaiah describes the new creation in the language of his own world: long life is a picture of life without loss. The words about death are a poetic way of saying that the curse is broken, not a literal statement that death continues.

Future-kingdom writers reply that this treats the clear words 'die' and 'sinner' as mere figures, while taking 'new heavens' literally in the same passage. Some, such as Blaising, suggest that Isaiah's 'new heavens and new earth' include both the millennium and the eternal state in one prophetic view, with the New Testament later separating the stages. This, they argue, is the same pattern by which the prophets merged the first and second comings.
Believers are already in the kingdom and are a kingdom of priests

Paul says the Father has rescued believers from the domain of darkness and transferred them into the kingdom of his beloved Son (Colossians 1:13); the verbs are past tense. John greets the churches as people Christ has made 'a kingdom, priests to his God and Father' (Revelation 1:5-6), and calls himself their partner in 'the tribulation and kingdom and patient endurance' (Revelation 1:9). Peter applies Israel's Sinai title, 'a kingdom of priests and a holy nation' (Exodus 19:6), to the scattered church (1 Peter 2:9). The present-kingdom reading holds that the church is not waiting to enter a kingdom; it is already the kingdom's people.

Future-kingdom writers agree that believers share a present spiritual kingdom, but they point out that Revelation 5:10 promises the saints that they 'shall reign on the earth', which they see as a future reign. Dispensationalists also hold that applying Israel's titles to the church is a matter of analogy or shared blessing, not a transfer of identity; the church is like Israel in some ways without becoming Israel.

Present-kingdom writers note that Revelation 5:10 has a textual variant: Codex Alexandrinus and many later manuscripts read 'they reign' (present tense), while other manuscripts read 'they will reign'; the reading is disputed. Even with the future tense, the reign 'on the earth' can be the reign in the new earth of Revelation 21-22. They also argue that Peter does not say the church is 'like' Israel; he gives it Israel's own titles without qualification.
Zechariah 14: the Lord's feet on the Mount of Olives

Zechariah 14:4 says that on that day the Lord's feet will stand on the Mount of Olives, which will split in two. Zechariah 14:9 says the Lord will be king over all the earth. Zechariah 14:16-19 says the survivors of the nations that attacked Jerusalem will go up each year to worship the King and to keep the Feast of Tabernacles, and that nations who refuse will have no rain. Future-kingdom writers note that Acts 1:11-12 links Christ's return to the Mount of Olives, and argue that a world with nations, rain, punishment and annual pilgrimage to Jerusalem is not the eternal state. It describes a millennial reign on this earth.

Present-kingdom writers answer that Zechariah describes the final victory in the forms of worship known in his own time, as the prophets always did. The Feast of Tabernacles celebrated the final harvest and God dwelling with his people; John 7:37-39 and Revelation 7:9-17 (palm branches, God spreading his tent over them) apply that feast to Christ and the Spirit. A return to the Mosaic festival calendar would contradict Colossians 2:16-17, which calls such feasts a shadow of Christ.

Future-kingdom writers reply that Zechariah gives concrete geography, a named mountain and a specific direction of splitting, which is hard to treat as symbol. They argue that memorial feasts in the millennium need not be a return to the law, just as the Lord's Supper is a memorial now. Baldwin and others note that the passage is difficult for every school, but they hold that the literal reading leaves fewer details unexplained.
Seated now, far above every rule and authority

Paul says God raised Christ and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above every ruler, authority, power and name, in this age and the age to come, and put all things under his feet (Ephesians 1:20-22). Jesus himself says all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him (Matthew 28:18). Psalms 110:2 pictures the king ruling 'in the midst of your enemies', which describes a reign in a world where opposition continues. The present-kingdom reading holds that Christ already holds the highest rule possible; no future earthly throne could raise him higher.

Future-kingdom writers answer that Hebrews 2:8 openly says 'we do not yet see all things put under him'. Christ has the right to rule, but the actual subjection of the nations is still future. Hebrews 10:12-13 says he is 'waiting' until his enemies are made his footstool, which, they argue, describes a period before his active reign over the earth begins.

Present-kingdom writers reply that 'waiting' in Hebrews 10:13 is the waiting of a seated, reigning king, as in Psalms 110:1-2, where the king already rules while the enemies are being subdued. Hebrews 2:8-9 sets 'we do not yet see' against 'but we see Jesus crowned with glory and honour'. The 'not yet' is the full display at his return, and Hebrews places that display in the coming world and the unshakable kingdom (Hebrews 12:26-28), not in an earthly interim.
Revelation 20:1-6: a thousand years after the return

In the order of John's visions, Christ returns on the white horse and defeats the beast and the false prophet (Revelation 19:11-21). Then an angel binds Satan for a thousand years (Revelation 20:1-3), the martyrs 'came to life and reigned with Christ a thousand years' (20:4), and 'the rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were ended' (20:5). Future-kingdom writers hold that the plainest reading is a sequence: return, binding, a reign of a thousand years, then a final rebellion and judgment. Ladd argued that if the same verb means bodily resurrection in verse 5, it must mean bodily resurrection in verse 4.
